en: Thus have I heard: The Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta, Discourse 90 of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruññā in the Kaṇṇakatthala Deer Park.
Now on that occasion King Pasenadi of Kosala had arrived at Uruññā for some business or other.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man:

“Come, good man, go to where the Blessed One is. Having approached, pay homage with your head at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, and inquire after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical vigor, strength, and well-being, saying:

‘Venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and inquires after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical vigor, strength, and well-being.
And speak thus:”
“Venerable sir, it is said that today, after his meal and having finished his breakfast, King Pasenadi of Kosala will approach the Blessed One for an audience.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” that man replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala.
He then went to the Blessed One, and having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. To one side...
Seated there, that man said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala pays homage with his head at the feet of the Blessed One; he inquires after your health, freedom from illness, physical lightness, strength, and well-being, and he says this:”
“Venerable sir, today King Pasenadi of Kosala, having finished his morning meal after the midday meal, will approach the Blessed One for an audience.
The sisters Somā and Sakulā heard:
“Today King Pasenadi of Kosala, having finished his morning meal after the midday meal, will approach the Blessed One for an audience.”
Then the sisters Soma and Sakulā approached King Pasenadi of Kosala while he was having his meal and said this to him:

“In that case, Great King, on our behalf as well, pay homage with your head at the feet of the Blessed One, and inquire after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and comfortable dwelling, saying:

‘Venerable Sir, the sisters Soma and Sakulā pay homage with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One; they inquire after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and comfortable dwelling.’”
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having finished his meal and eaten his breakfast, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the sisters Somā and Sakulā pay homage with their heads at the Blessed One’s feet; they inquire after his health, freedom from affliction, lightness of body, strength, and well-being.
“But why, great king, did the sisters Somā and Sakulā not find another messenger?
“Venerable sir, the sisters Somā and Sakulā heard this:”
‘Today, it seems, King Pasenadi of Kosala, having finished his meal after breakfast, will approach the Blessed One for a visit.
Then, Bhante, the sisters Somā and Sakulā came to me while I was being served my meal and said this:

‘In that case, Great King, on our behalf as well, pay homage with your head at the feet of the Blessed One, and inquire after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness of body, strength, and comfortable dwelling.’”
“Somā, your sister, and Sakulā, your sister, bow their heads at the Blessed One’s feet; they inquire after your health, freedom from illness, physical ease, strength, and well-being.
“May they both be well, Great King—both Somā, your sister, and Sakulā, your sister.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The ascetic Gotama has said:
“There is no ascetic or brahmin who, being all-knowing and all-seeing, would claim to possess knowledge and vision without remainder; such a thing is impossible.
Bhante, as for those who say this: ‘The ascetic Gotama has said—there is no ascetic or brahmin who...’”
‘It is impossible that one who claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, and to possess knowledge and vision without exception—this cannot be’;
do you, venerable sir, speak as the Blessed One has spoken, and do you not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false?
Do you explain in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no legitimate criticism can be brought against you?”
“Great King, those who say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama says thus:
"There is no ascetic or brahmin who is all-knowing and all-seeing and who can claim to possess knowledge and vision without remainder;
such a thing is impossible,"'—they do not speak my words, and they misrepresent me with what is false and untrue.”
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed his general Viḍūḍabha:
"General, who was it that introduced this subject of conversation into the royal palace?
"It was the brahmin Sañjaya, sire, of the Ākāsa clan."
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man:
“Come, good man, in my name address the brahmin Sañjaya of the Ākāsa clan, saying:
‘Venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala calls for you.’”
“Yes, sire,” that man replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala. He approached the brahmin Sañjaya of the Ākāsa clan and, having approached him, said to the brahmin Sañjaya of the Ākāsa clan:
“Venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala summons you.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it may be that the Blessed One spoke with something else in mind, yet people might understand it otherwise.
In what way, venerable sir, does the Blessed One recall having spoken such words?
“It is indeed so, great king, that I recall having spoken these words:”
“There is no such recluse or brahmin who could know all at once, who could see all at once; such a thing is impossible.
“The Blessed One has spoken what is reasonable, venerable sir; the Blessed One has spoken what is well-founded when he said:
‘There is no such recluse or brahmin who could know all at once, who could see all at once; such a thing is impossible.’”
“Venerable sir, there are these four castes—
the khattiyas, the brahmins, the vessas,
and the suddas. Now, venerable sir, could there be any distinction, any difference between these four castes?”
“Great King, there are these four castes:
khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, and suddas.
Of these four castes, Great King, two castes are declared to be the highest: [the khattiyas and the brahmins].”
“Khattiyas and brahmins—
that is to say, acts of salutation, rising from one’s seat, joining the palms in reverential salutation,
and performing duties of respect. “Venerable sir, I am not asking the Blessed One about matters pertaining to the present life;”
"I ask the Blessed One, venerable sir, concerning the future life.
There are these four castes, venerable sir:
khattiyas, brāhmaṇas, vessas, and suddas."
“Venerable sir, might there be some distinction, some difference between these four castes?
“Great king, there are these five factors of striving. Which five? [The Blessed One continued:]”
In this case, great king, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus:

“The Blessed One is indeed an arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He is free from illness and affliction, possessed of a healthy digestion that is neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and fit for exertion.
He is not fraudulent, he is not deceitful, and he reveals himself as he truly is to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.

He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
These, O Great King, are the five factors of striving.
There are these four castes, O Great King:
Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, and Suddas.
“Indeed, if they were endowed with these five factors of striving,
it would lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time. “There are,
venerable sir, these four castes:”
“Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, and suddas.
Suppose they were all endowed with these five factors of striving;
in that case, venerable sir, would there be any distinction or any difference among them?”
“In this regard, Great King, I speak of a difference in their application of effort.

Suppose, Great King, there were two well-trained and well-disciplined elephant-tamers, horse-tamers, or cow-tamers, and two elephant-tamers, horse-tamers, or cow-tamers who were untamed and undisciplined.
What do you think, Great King?”

“Suppose there were two elephant-tamers, or horse-tamers, or ox-tamers, who had well-tamed and well-trained [animals]. Would those [animals] go to the place for the tamed because they are indeed tamed, and would they reach the stage of being tamed because they are indeed tamed?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“But as for those two elephant-tamers, or horse-tamers, or ox-tamers, who have [animals] that are untamed and untrained, would they [go to the place for the tamed]?”
“Would those who are untamed go to the place for taming, and would those who are untamed reach the ground of the tamed,
just as those two well-tamed and well-trained elephant-riders, horse-riders, or ox-riders?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“In the same way, Great King, it is impossible that one who lacks faith, is frequently ill, is fraudulent, deceitful, lazy,
and lacking in wisdom should attain what is to be attained by one who has faith, is free from illness, is not fraudulent, is not deceitful, is energetic, and is wise.”
“Venerable sir, the Blessed One has spoken of the nature of cause; venerable sir, the Blessed One has spoken of the nature of having a cause.
There are these four castes, venerable sir:
khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, and suddas.”
“Suppose, venerable sir, that these people were endowed with these five factors of striving and were practicing right effort;
in this regard, sir, would there be any distinction or any difference between them?
“In this matter, great king, I say there is no distinction whatsoever between them—namely, liberation compared to liberation.”
"Just as, great king, a man might take a dry branch of a *sāka* tree and produce fire, manifesting heat;
then another man might take a dry branch of a *sāla* tree and produce fire, manifesting heat;
and then another man might take a dry branch of a mango tree and produce fire, manifesting heat."
"Then suppose another person were to take a dry piece of fig wood and produce fire,
manifesting heat. What do you think, Great King,
would there be any difference between those fires produced from various kinds of wood— in terms of flame compared to flame, color compared to color, or radiance compared to radiance?"
“No, venerable sir.

“In the same way, great king, regarding that fire produced by exertion and generated through striving, I do not say there is any difference between it and liberation—that is, liberation is liberation.
“The Blessed One has spoken what is reasonable, venerable sir; the Blessed One has spoken what is well-founded, venerable sir.”
"But, venerable sir, are there gods?
"But why do you say this, great king:
'But, venerable sir, are there gods'?"
“Venerable sir, will those gods come to this state, or will they not come to this state?
“Great king, those gods who possess affliction will come to this state; those gods who are free from affliction will not come to this state.
When this was said, the general Viṭaṭūbha addressed the Blessed One as follows:

“Venerable sir, will those gods who are subject to affliction and are destined to return to this state of existence be displaced or expelled from their place by those gods who are free from affliction and are not destined to return to this state of existence?
Then, it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“This General Viṭaṭūbha is the son of King Pasenadi of Kosala.”
“I am the Blessed One’s son.
This is the time for a father and son to converse.
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the general Viṭaṭūbha:
“In that case, general, I shall question you about this very matter; answer as you see fit.
What do you think, general:
as far as the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala extends, and wherever King Pasenadi of Kosala exercises sovereign power—”
"He rules the kingdom; is King Pasenadi of Kosala able there to remove from that position, or to banish, any ascetic or brahmin—
whether meritorious or demeritorious, whether leading a holy life or not leading a holy life?"
“Sir, as far as the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala extends, and wherever King Pasenadi of Kosala exercises his sovereignty,
lordship, and kingship, there King Pasenadi of Kosala is capable of [punishing] any ascetic or brahmin—
whether they possess merit or lack merit, whether they lead the holy life or do not lead the holy life— from that [place].”
“...to move him from his position or to ordain him.
“What do you think, general?
As far as King Pasenadi of Kosala has not conquered, and wherever King Pasenadi of Kosala does not exercise sovereign power—”
“Does King Pasenadi of Kosala exercise sovereignty there, such that he is able to remove from his position or cause to go forth into homelessness any ascetic or brahmin—
whether meritorious or demeritorious, whether leading a holy life or not leading a holy life?”
“To whatever extent, sir, there is that which has not been conquered by King Pasenadi of Kosala,
and wherever King Pasenadi of Kosala does not exercise sovereignty, lordship, and rule— therein King Pasenadi of Kosala is not able [to influence] whether it be a recluse or a brahmin,
whether they be meritorious or demeritorious, or whether they lead the holy life or do not lead the holy life.”
“Or to displace him from that place or to cause him to go forth?
“What do you think, general,
have you heard of the Tāvatiṃsa devas?”
“Yes, sir.
I have heard of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Your majesty, King Pasenadi of Kosala has also heard of the Tāvatiṃsa devas here.”
“What do you think, general, is King Pasenadi of Kosala able to displace the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven from that place, or to cause them to go forth?
“Sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala is not even able to see the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; how much less could he displace them from that place or cause them to go forth?”
“In the same way, general, those gods who are subject to affliction and are subject to return to this state cannot even see those gods who are free from affliction and do not return to this state;
how much less could they displace them from that place or expel them?”
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, what is the name of this bhikkhu?
"His name is Ānanda, Great King."
“Truly, sir, Ānanda is joyful; truly, sir, Ānanda has a joyful nature.
Venerable sir, the Venerable Ānanda has spoken with reason; venerable sir, the Venerable Ānanda has spoken with good cause.
But, venerable sir, does Brahmā exist?”
“But why, Great King, do you say this:
‘But, venerable sir, does Brahmā exist?
‘Venerable sir, whether that Brahmā comes to this state of existence, or whether he does not come to this state of existence.’”
“Great King, that Brahmā who is subject to affliction, that Brahmā will come to this state; that Brahmā who is free from affliction, that Brahmā will not come to this state.
Then a certain man said to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“Great King, the brahmin Sañjaya of the Ākāsa clan has arrived.”
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the brahmin Sañjaya of the Ākāsa clan:
"Brahmin, who was it that first introduced this subject of conversation into the royal palace?
"It was Viṭaṭūbha, the commander-in-chief, Great King."
The general Viṭaṭūbha spoke thus:
“Great King, the brahmin Sañjaya is of the Ākāsagotta clan.
Then a certain man said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“It is time for the vehicle, Great King.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, we asked the Blessed One about omniscience, and the Blessed One has explained omniscience to us.”
And that indeed is pleasing and acceptable to us, and for that we are glad.
We asked the Blessed One, venerable sir, about the purification of the four castes, and the Blessed One has explained the purification of the four castes;
and that indeed is pleasing and acceptable to us, and for that we are glad.
"Venerable sir, we questioned the Blessed One concerning the supreme deity, and the Blessed One has answered concerning the supreme deity;
that is pleasing and acceptable to us, and therefore we are uplifted in mind.
Venerable sir, we questioned the Blessed One concerning the supreme Brahmā, and the Blessed One has answered concerning the supreme Brahmā."
And that indeed is pleasing and acceptable to us, and for that reason we are glad.
Whatever we asked the Blessed One, that very thing the Blessed One has explained;
and that indeed is pleasing and acceptable to us, and for that reason we are glad.
“And now, venerable sir, we depart;
we have many duties and much to do.
“Now is the time for you to do as you think fit, great king,” he replied.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
The *Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta*, the tenth, is finished.
The fourth chapter, the *Rājavagga*, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Ghaṭīkāra, Raṭṭhapāla,
Maghadeva, and Madhurika.
Bodhi and Aṅgulimāla,
Piya, Jātaka, Bāhitika;
and the Dhammacetiyasutta—
The tenth is Kaṇṇakatthala.
